topic: resetting the boulder problems on a small community climbing wall

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is sorting and costing the problem list, base is a conversation about why beginners avoid the easy end

a: Here are eight new boulder problems with their grades: three, four, four, five, five, six, six, seven.
Each problem uses a different number of holds: nine, eleven, eight, fourteen, twelve, sixteen, fifteen, and nineteen.
Pair each grade with its hold count and sort the list by grade, lowest first.
Then give me the average number of holds for the problems at grade five and below.
Finish with the total number of holds used across all eight problems on the wall.
base: We reset the main wall last weekend, and the easy end of the grid is being ignored.
Beginners walk past the low problems, cross the room, and head for the steep back corner.
Then they fall off everything there, rest for a while, and leave without climbing very much.
The low problems are on the slab, which is where we have always put them.
Is the slab itself the problem, or is it the way the grid is laid out?

a: Sorted by grade, lowest first: grade three with nine holds, then grade four with eleven holds.
Then grade four with eight holds, grade five with fourteen holds, and grade five with twelve.
Grade six follows with sixteen holds, grade six with fifteen holds, and grade seven with nineteen.
The average at grade five and below is fifty-four holds over five problems, so ten point eight.
The total across all eight problems is one hundred four holds on the wall.
base: The slab is very likely the problem, because slab climbing punishes beginners with fear rather than strength.
A new climber has no foot confidence yet, and a slab asks for exactly that.
Put the easiest problems on a gentle overhang instead, where the hands take some of the weight.
It feels harder to a strong climber but reads as friendlier to a nervous one.
How much gently overhanging wall do you actually have in that room at present?

a: Now group the eight problems by colour: red, red, blue, blue, blue, blue, yellow, and green.
The colours follow the same order as the grades I gave you at the start.
List each colour with the grades it covers and the number of problems in it.
Then tell me which colour spans the widest range of grades on the wall.
Give the hold count per colour as a total, not as an average per problem.
base: There is about four metres of wall at twenty degrees, next to the training board.
It is the least used part of the room, mostly because nothing is ever set there.
We keep the twenty degree section for the strong regulars who ask for hard problems.
Moving beginners onto it would mean pushing those problems somewhere else entirely.
Where would the hard problems go if the gentle overhang became the beginner area?

a: Red covers grades three and four, with two problems and twenty holds in total.
Blue covers grades four, five, five, and six, with four problems and fifty holds.
Yellow is one problem at grade six with fifteen holds, and green one problem at seven.
Green uses nineteen holds, which makes it the most hold-heavy problem on the whole wall.
Blue spans the widest range, covering three grades from four to six across four problems.
base: Move the hard problems onto the training board side and the steep corner at the back.
Strong climbers will find them anywhere; a nervous beginner will not go looking at all.
Keep the first four problems within three steps of the door, where people can watch.
Visibility matters more than angle for a first session, because people copy what they see.
Do you set the easy problems with the same holds as the hard ones?

a: One change: the green problem is grade eight, not seven, and it now uses twenty-one holds.
Update the total hold count and the green entry, leaving all other colours as they are.
Then tell me the new average number of holds across all eight problems on the wall.
Round that average to one decimal place and give me the range of grades present.
Also list how many problems sit at grade five or above after this change.
base: We use the same holds for everything, whatever comes out of the bins that day.
The bins are sorted by colour rather than by size, which nobody has ever questioned.
So a beginner problem can end up on small crimps if that is what the bin holds.
It never seemed important because the moves themselves were easy on the slab.
Should the easy problems have their own set of holds kept separately from the rest?

a: Green becomes grade eight with twenty-one holds, so the total rises to one hundred six.
Red, blue, and yellow are unchanged at twenty, fifty, and fifteen holds respectively.
The new average is one hundred six divided by eight, which is thirteen point three.
The grade range now runs from three to eight, a span of five grades in all.
Five problems sit at grade five or above: two at five, two at six, one at eight.
base: Yes, keep a separate stock of large, positive holds for the first three grades.
Beginners need something they can hold without gripping hard, in almost any hand position.
Sort those bins by shape rather than colour, since shape is what the hand meets.
Colour only matters for reading the line from the floor, not for climbing the move.
Would your setters accept sorting the store by shape if you relabelled the bins?

a: Give me a setting schedule for eight problems over four sessions, two problems per session.
Pair one easy problem with one hard problem in every session, using the grades above.
List each session with its two grades and the total holds needed for that session.
Order the sessions so the hardest pair comes last and the easiest pair comes first.
Assume two setters work three hours per session and tell me the total setter hours.
base: The setters would accept it, though the store is small and the shelves are already full.
Relabelling would take an evening, and someone would have to keep it tidy afterwards.
That has never lasted more than a month with anything else we have organised there.
The bins get emptied onto the floor during a reset and refilled in a hurry.
How do other walls stop the store falling back into a heap after every reset?

a: Session one takes grade three with nine holds and grade five with fourteen, twenty-three in total.
Session two takes grade four with eleven holds and grade five with twelve, twenty-three in total.
Session three takes grade four with eight holds and grade six with sixteen, twenty-four in total.
Session four takes grade six with fifteen holds and grade eight with twenty-one, thirty-six in total.
Two setters over four sessions of three hours each gives twenty-four setter hours in all.
base: The ones that hold up put the bins on wheels and roll them to the wall.
Holds go back into the bin they came from because the bin is right there.
A shelf across the room guarantees a heap on the floor by the second hour.
Label the bins by shape with a photograph, not a name, so sorting needs no reading.
Then one person can tidy the whole store in ten minutes at the end.

a: Convert the setter hours into cost at eighteen pounds per hour and give me the total.
Then split that cost across the four sessions and tell me the cost per problem.
Add sixty pounds of new holds per session and give me the full project cost.
Give the figures rounded to whole pounds, with no decimals anywhere in the list.
Finish with the cost per problem including holds, again rounded to whole pounds.
base: Wheeled bins would fit, and there is an old trolley in the plant room downstairs.
Photographs on the bins is the part I like most, since half our setters are volunteers.
They come once a month and forget where everything lives between one reset and the next.
A picture would survive that gap much better than a name written on tape.
Is there anything else worth photographing while we are down there with a camera?

a: Twenty-four setter hours at eighteen pounds gives four hundred thirty-two pounds of labour cost.
Split across four sessions that is one hundred eight pounds per session for labour.
Labour per problem is fifty-four pounds, since each session produces exactly two problems.
Holds add sixty pounds per session, or two hundred forty pounds across the project.
Total project cost is six hundred seventy-two pounds, which is eighty-four pounds per problem.
base: Photograph the wall itself before you strip it, panel by panel with the holds on.
You lose the record of every line the moment the first hold comes off.
A set of panel photographs also shows which bolt holes are wearing out.
Then photograph the finished set so people can find a problem after it is gone.
Those two habits cost nothing and settle half the arguments that come up later.
